name: Siddhāsana (the adept's seat)
method_summary: Seated with the heel of one foot pressing the perineum (yonisthāna) and the other foot placed above the genitals, body straight, chin on the chest (a form of jālandhara), senses restrained and the gaze fixed between the brows (HYP 1.35; GS 2.7; ŚS 3.85; GŚ 8). A second arrangement with the left ankle above the genitals is given 'by another view' (HYP 1.36). The texts call it the chief of postures, the one to sit in always.

names.name: vajrāsana / muktāsana / guptāsana (other names reported in HYP 1.37)

signs_of_progress: purifies the 72,000 channels (HYP 1.39)
with it kevala kumbhaka, unmanī and the three locks arise spontaneously (HYP 1.41-42)
practised with moderate diet and meditation on the self for twelve years it brings completion (HYP 1.40)
breaks open the door of liberation (HYP 1.35; GS 2.7)
duration: the HYP (1.40) speaks of twelve years of practice for completion

HYP 1.37 reports the name muktāsana for it; GS 2.11 describes muktāsana separately.
HYP 1.37 reports the name guptāsana for it; GS 2.20 describes guptāsana separately.

name: Padmāsana (the lotus seat)
method_summary: Each foot placed on the opposite thigh. In the 'bound' form the hands cross behind the back to hold the big toes, the chin rests on the chest and the gaze is on the nose-tip (HYP 1.44; GS 2.8). In another form the soles are upturned on the thighs, the hands palms-up between the thighs, the gaze on the nose-tip, the tongue at the root of the front teeth and the breath drawn in slowly (HYP 1.45-47; DYŚ 31-35; ŚS 3.88-91). It is the seat for breath-practice in many texts (HYP 2.7, 2.59).
signs_of_progress: destroys all diseases (HYP 1.44, 1.47; DYŚ 35)
with prāṇa and apāna united in it, awakening through the power of śakti (HYP 1.48)
one who holds the breath in it is liberated (HYP 1.49)
notes: Listed in the Yoga-bhāṣya on YS 2.46. U10's paraphrase of that list omits vīrāsana; the unit recalls 'padmāsanaṃ vīrāsanaṃ bhadrāsanaṃ svastikaṃ …' — check the bhāṣya. Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Baddhapadmāsana (the bound lotus)
method_summary: Padmāsana with the arms crossed behind the back holding the big toes (HYP 1.44; GS 2.8); named as the seat for purifying the channels (HYP 2.7; GŚ 41, 43) and in Dattātreya's own posture (DYŚ 5).
notes: The Triśikhibrāhmaṇa lists baddhapadma separately from padma.

name: Siṃhāsana (the lion seat)
method_summary: The ankles placed under the scrotum at the sides of the perineum, crossed (left to the right side, right to the left), the hands on the knees with fingers spread, the mouth open, gazing at the nose-tip (HYP 1.50-52); in the Gheraṇḍa the knees rest on the ground and jālandhara is applied (GS 2.14-15).
signs_of_progress: brings about the three locks (HYP 1.52)
destroys all diseases (GS 2.15)
notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Bhadrāsana (the auspicious seat)
method_summary: The ankles under the scrotum at the sides of the perineum, the sides of the feet held firmly with the hands (HYP 1.53-54); in the Gheraṇḍa the ankles are crossed, the big toes held from behind, jālandhara applied and the gaze on the nose-tip (GS 2.9-10).
signs_of_progress: destroys all diseases (HYP 1.54; GS 2.10)

name: Svastikāsana (the auspicious-mark seat)
method_summary: Both soles placed between the knees and thighs, sitting with the body straight (HYP 1.19; GS 2.13; ŚS 3.95). The Śivasaṃhitā calls it the comfortable posture (sukhāsana).
signs_of_progress: no disease enters the body and the breath is mastered (ŚS 3.96)

name: Gomukhāsana (the cow-face seat)
method_summary: The right ankle set beside the left buttock and the left beside the right, so that the legs resemble a cow's face (HYP 1.20); in the Gheraṇḍa the feet are on the ground with the heels by the sides of the back and the body steady (GS 2.16).
notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra. The Śivasaṃhitā (5.5) counts 'sitting in gomukha' among the obstacles that take the form of knowledge.

name: Vīrāsana (the hero's seat)
method_summary: One foot set firmly on the other thigh and the other thigh on the other foot (HYP 1.21); in the Gheraṇḍa one foot on the thigh and the other turned back (GS 2.17).

name: Muktāsana (the free seat)
method_summary: The left ankle at the root of the anus and the right ankle above it, with head, neck and body in line (GS 2.11); HYP 1.37 gives muktāsana as another name of siddhāsana; the Haṭhapradīpikā has the yogin sit in muktāsana to listen to the inner sound (HYP 4.67).
signs_of_progress: gives success (GS 2.11)

name: Vajrāsana (the thunderbolt seat)
method_summary: The thighs made firm like a thunderbolt and the feet placed by the sides of the anus (GS 2.12); it is the seat for khecarī in the Śivasaṃhitā (4.31) and for śakticālana in the Haṭhapradīpikā (3.114-115). HYP 1.37 records vajrāsana as another name for siddhāsana.
signs_of_progress: gives success to yogins (GS 2.12)

name: Guptāsana (the hidden seat)
method_summary: The feet hidden between the knees and thighs and the anus placed on the feet (GS 2.20); HYP 1.37 gives guptāsana as another name of siddhāsana.

name: Sukhāsana (the comfortable seat)
method_summary: A comfortable seated posture: in the Śivasaṃhitā the name is given to svastika (ŚS 3.97); the Gheraṇḍa has sagarbha breath-control done 'seated in sukhāsana' (GS 5.49); the Darśana and Triśikhibrāhmaṇa Upaniṣads list sukha among their postures.

name: Yogāsana (the yoga seat)
method_summary: The feet, turned up, placed on the knees and the hands, turned up, on the seat, drawing in the breath and gazing at the nose-tip — a posture for yoga-practice (GS 2.44-45); also listed in the Triśikhibrāhmaṇa.

name: Gorakṣāsana (Gorakṣa's seat)
method_summary: The feet turned up between the knees and thighs, the heels covered with the upturned hands, the throat contracted and the gaze on the nose-tip (GS 2.24-25). In HYP 1.54 'gorakṣāsana' is the siddhas' name for bhadrāsana.
signs_of_progress: a cause of success for yogins (GS 2.25)

name: Kūrmāsana (the tortoise seat)
method_summary: The anus closed firmly with the ankles placed in reverse order (HYP 1.22); in the Gheraṇḍa the ankles crossed under the scrotum with body, head and neck straight (GS 2.32).

name: Matsyendrāsana (Matsyendra's seat)
method_summary: A seated twist: one foot at the root of the opposite thigh and the other wound outside the knee, the body turned and the feet held (HYP 1.26); in the Gheraṇḍa the left foot is placed on the right knee, the right elbow set on it, the face resting on the right hand and the gaze between the brows (GS 2.22-23).
signs_of_progress: kindles the digestive fire, destroys terrible diseases, awakens kuṇḍalinī and steadies the moon (HYP 1.27)

name: Paścimatānāsana (the stretch of the back; paścimottāna, ugrāsana)
method_summary: The legs stretched on the ground like a staff, the tips of the feet held with the hands and the forehead brought to the knees (HYP 1.28; GS 2.26). The Śivasaṃhitā's 'fierce posture' (ugrāsana), with the legs apart and the head on the knees, is expressly identified with paścimottāna (ŚS 3.92). It is also the base for dry basti and taḍāgī mudrā (GS 1.48, 3.61).
signs_of_progress: makes the breath flow in the back (central) channel, kindles the digestive fire, slims the belly, gives health (HYP 1.29)
kindles the breath and removes bodily decline (ŚS 3.92)

name: Utkaṭāsana (the squat on the toes)
method_summary: The ground supported by the toes, the heels raised, the anus set upon the heels (GS 2.27). It is the posture taken in water for basti (HYP 2.26; GS 1.46).

name: Saṅkaṭāsana (the constricted seat)
method_summary: The left leg set on the ground and the right leg wound around the left, with the hands on the knees (GS 2.28).
notes: The e-text wording is terse; details of the leg placement are uncertain.

name: Vṛṣāsana (the bull seat)
method_summary: The anus set on the right ankle and the other foot, turned the other way, on the left side touching the ground (GS 2.38).

name: Garuḍāsana (the Garuḍa seat)
method_summary: Pressing the ground with shins and thighs, the body steadied by the knees, the hands on the knees (GS 2.37).
notes: The Gheraṇḍa's garuḍāsana is not the modern standing posture of the same name.

name: Maṇḍūkāsana (the frog)
method_summary: The soles turned back, the big toes touching and the knees set forward (GS 2.34).

name: Uttānamaṇḍūkāsana (the supine frog)
method_summary: From the frog posture, holding the head with the elbows and lying back like a frog (GS 2.35).

name: Matsyāsana (the fish)
method_summary: In the lotus with the feet free (muktapadmāsana), lying supine and encircling the head with the elbows (GS 2.21); also listed in the Triśikhibrāhmaṇa.
signs_of_progress: destroys disease (GS 2.21)

name: Kukkuṭāsana (the cockerel)
method_summary: From padmāsana the hands are inserted between the knees and thighs, planted on the ground, and the body raised into the air (HYP 1.23; GS 2.31).

name: Uttānakūrmāsana (the supine tortoise)
method_summary: From the bound kukkuṭa position the neck is clasped with the arms and one lies back like a tortoise on its back (HYP 1.24; GS 2.33).

name: Mayūrāsana (the peacock)
method_summary: The palms pressed to the ground, the sides of the navel resting on the elbows, the body raised horizontal in the air like a staff (HYP 1.30; GS 2.29).
signs_of_progress: quickly removes gulma, abdominal swellings and other diseases; overcomes the doṣas; 'burns up' bad food; kindles the digestive fire; digests even the poison kālakūṭa (HYP 1.31; GS 2.30)
notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Dhanurāsana (the bow)
method_summary: In the Haṭhapradīpikā the big toes are held with the hands and drawn up to the ear like a drawn bow (HYP 1.25); in the Gheraṇḍa the legs are stretched on the ground, the feet held from behind and the body curved like a bow (GS 2.18).
notes: The two texts describe different forms under one name.

name: Śavāsana (the corpse; mṛtāsana)
method_summary: Lying supine on the ground like a corpse (HYP 1.32; GS 2.19); the Dattātreyayogaśāstra counts lying like a corpse, relaxed in solitude, among the 'signals' of laya-yoga (DYŚ 22-23).
signs_of_progress: removes fatigue and brings rest to the mind (HYP 1.32; GS 2.19)
notes: Later 'yoga-nidrā' teachings built on this posture belong to recent lineages (U52).

name: Śalabhāsana (the locust)
method_summary: Lying face down with the hands (palms) on the ground by the chest, the feet raised a span into the air (GS 2.39).

name: Makarāsana (the crocodile)
method_summary: Lying face down with the chest on the ground and the legs stretched out, the head held with the arms (GS 2.40).
signs_of_progress: increases the bodily fire (GS 2.40)

name: Uṣṭrāsana (the camel)
method_summary: Lying face down, the feet turned up behind and held with the hands, the mouth and belly firmly contracted (GS 2.41).
notes: The Gheraṇḍa's form is prone, unlike the modern kneeling posture of this name.

name: Bhujaṅgāsana (the serpent)
method_summary: From the toes to the navel the body rests on the ground; supporting the ground with the palms one raises the head like a serpent (GS 2.42-43).
signs_of_progress: the bodily fire increases, all diseases are destroyed and the serpent goddess (kuṇḍalinī) awakens (GS 2.43)

name: Vṛkṣāsana (the tree)
method_summary: Standing on the left leg with the right foot set at the root of the left thigh, like a tree (GS 2.36).

name: The postures of the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati (group entry)
method_summary: A prose haṭha manual that describes more than a hundred postures (about 112 are counted), set in a sequence after the yamas, niyamas and cleansing acts and before breath-control and mudrā; many are dynamic or repeated movements and some use a rope. Its postures reappear, illustrated, in the Mysore Śrītattvanidhi. The individual names are not recalled with enough confidence to be entered here (see REPORT).
notes: Group entry standing in for the individual postures the unit could not responsibly name.

name: The eighty-four postures of the Jogapradīpikā (group entry)
method_summary: The Brajbhāṣā Jogapradīpikā (18th c.) teaches eighty-four postures, alongside mudrās and other practices; the individual names are not recalled with enough confidence to be entered here.

name: The eighty-four postures of the Haṭharatnāvalī (group entry)
method_summary: The Haṭharatnāvalī (ch. 3) names eighty-four postures and describes a selection, repeating the Haṭhapradīpikā's descriptions for several (siddha, padma, siṃha, bhadra and others) and adding many variants; the full list is not entered here because the unit could not recall it reliably (see REPORT for candidate names to check).

name: Breath-control (prāṇāyāma) in haṭha
method_summary: In the haṭha texts breath-control is exhalation, inhalation and retention (kumbhaka), retention being either sahita (joined with inhalation and exhalation) or kevala (without them) (HYP 2.71). Because mind moves with breath (HYP 2.2), holding the breath steadies the mind; with the channels purified and the three locks applied the breath enters the suṣumnā and the state of manonmanī arises (HYP 2.41-42, 2.45-47). It follows firm posture and is practised as the guru teaches (HYP 2.1); the Gheraṇḍa makes place, season, moderate diet and purification of the channels its preliminaries (GS 5.2). Grades are known by sweat, trembling and rising from the ground (HYP 2.12; GS 5.56-57; ŚS 3.40-46; GŚ 49).
prerequisites: place, season and purification of the channels (GS 5.2)
signs_of_progress: lowest grade: sweat; middle: trembling; highest: the breath reaches its place / the body rises (HYP 2.12; GS 5.57)
steadiness of mind, manonmanī (HYP 2.42)
powers of moving in the sky, destruction of disease, awakening of the power (GS 5.58)

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.
Breath-control is to be practised by the path the guru teaches, once posture is firm and the diet wholesome and moderate.
Yoga begun in the cold, hot or rainy seasons, or without moderate diet, brings disease; begin in spring or autumn.
Release, fill and bind the breath each with due care; thus success comes.

name: Purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana, nāḍī-śuddhi)
method_summary: Alternate-nostril breathing with retention: inhaling through the moon (left) nostril, holding as far as one is able, exhaling through the sun (right), then inhaling through the right and exhaling through the left, always inhaling through the nostril just used for exhaling, slowly and never forcefully (HYP 2.7-10; ŚS 3.20-26; DYŚ 55-61); the Gorakṣaśataka adds contemplation of the moon-disc and of the blazing sun-disc (GŚ 41-46). The Gheraṇḍa distinguishes samanu purification, done with seed-syllables of air, fire and moon, from nirmanu purification by the cleansing act of dhauti (GS 5.35-46). It is practised at four junctures of the day for a period of months (the counts the texts give are not reproduced).
prerequisites: for those with excess fat or phlegm, first the six acts (HYP 2.21)
duration: the texts say the channels are purified after about three months of regular practice (HYP 2.10; ŚS 3.26; DYŚ 61)
signs_of_progress: slimness and radiance of body, breath held at will, kindled digestive fire, manifestation of the inner sound, health (HYP 2.19-20)
lightness, radiance, increased fire, slimness (DYŚ 62-63)
even body, fragrance, beauty, mastery of voice — the beginning stage (ŚS 3.29-31)

destroys old age and death, awakens kuṇḍalinī, increases the bodily fire (GS 5.68-69)

name: Bhastrikā ('the bellows')
method_summary: Seated in padmāsana, the breath is expelled and drawn in forcefully through the nose again and again like a blacksmith's bellows, sounding in heart, throat and skull; when tired, one fills through the right nostril, holds with the nostrils closed and releases through the left (HYP 2.59-67; GS 5.76-78). The numbers of strokes and rounds given in the Gheraṇḍa are not reproduced.
signs_of_progress: removes vāta, pitta and kapha, increases the bodily fire, quickly awakens kuṇḍalinī, destroys the phlegm barring the mouth of the brahma-channel, pierces the three knots (HYP 2.65-67)

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.
When fatigue arises in the body the bellows-breathing is to give way to filling through the sun (right) nostril.

name: Bhrāmarī ('the bee')
method_summary: In the Haṭhapradīpikā, rapid inhalation with the sound of a male bee and very slow exhalation with the hum of a female bee (HYP 2.68). In the Gheraṇḍa, practised after midnight in silence with the ears closed, it becomes a practice of listening: the inner sounds are heard in the right ear, from crickets and flute to drums and vīṇā, and the mind dissolves in the light within the unstruck sound (GS 5.79-83); it is the Gheraṇḍa's means to nāda-samādhi (GS 7.5-6, 7.10-11).
signs_of_progress: a play of indescribable bliss in the minds of the best yogins (HYP 2.68)
the inner sounds, a light within the sound, dissolution of the mind — 'Viṣṇu's supreme state' (GS 5.80-83)

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.

name: Mūrcchā ('the swoon')
method_summary: RESTRICTED — summary only: a retention with a very firm throat-lock at the end of inhalation and slow exhalation, which the texts say makes the mind faint and gives happiness (HYP 2.69); in the Gheraṇḍa, the mind is set between the brows during an easy retention, abandoning all objects — 'the swoon of the mind' — and joined to the self (GS 5.84-85), the means to one of its six samādhis (GS 7.16).
signs_of_progress: the fainting of the mind gives happiness (HYP 2.69)
bliss from joining the mind to the self; samādhi (GS 5.85)

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.

name: Plāvinī ('the floating')
method_summary: The belly is filled with abundant air drawn in, so that one floats easily on deep water like a lotus leaf (HYP 2.70).

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.

notes: The method of filling the belly is not specified in the verse; later commentators explain it (not reproduced).

name: Sahita-kumbhaka (retention joined with inhalation and exhalation)
method_summary: Retention accompanied by inhalation and exhalation, to be practised until kevala is attained (HYP 2.71-72); in the Dattātreyayogaśāstra the alternate-nostril practice is itself called sahita (DYŚ 58-60). The Gheraṇḍa counts sahita as the first of its eight retentions, in two forms: sagarbha, with the seed-syllables a, u, m and meditation on Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra (rajas, sattva, tamas), and nirgarbha, without seed (GS 5.47-55). Restricted only as to the counts and ratios, which are not reproduced.

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.

name: Kevala-kumbhaka (retention alone)
method_summary: RESTRICTED — summary only: the easy holding of the breath free of inhalation and exhalation, the fruit of sahita practice (HYP 2.72-73); it is said to arise spontaneously with mastery of siddhāsana (HYP 1.41). The Gheraṇḍa's kevalī is a retention measured against the count of the ajapā, with daily increments at set times (GS 5.92-99; counts not reproduced). When it is mastered nothing in the three worlds is unattainable; kuṇḍalinī awakens and the suṣumnā is freed (HYP 2.74-75; DYŚ 67-68).
signs_of_progress: nothing in the three worlds is hard to attain; the state of rājayoga (HYP 2.74-75)
awakening of kuṇḍalinī, unobstructed suṣumnā (HYP 2.75)
sweat, trembling, frog-like hopping, rising from the ground (DYŚ 69-76; ŚS 3.40-46)

warnings.text: As a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed only slowly, so the breath must be brought under control gradually; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Proper breath-control destroys all disease; improper practice produces all disease — hiccup, asthma, cough and pains in the head, ears and eyes arise from the disturbed breath.
Draw the breath in slowly and release it slowly; do not hold it excessively nor release it quickly.
Powers that arise at this stage are obstacles; they are not to be displayed; the yogin should behave like a fool or a deaf man to hide them.

equivalents.note: Both are a suspension of breath beyond the phases of inhalation and exhalation; the Yoga Sūtra's 'fourth' is defined by going beyond the outer and inner spheres, the haṭha kevala by the absence of inhalation and exhalation. The texts do not themselves identify them.

name: Kākī mudrā ('the crow')
method_summary: The mouth is shaped like a crow's beak and air is drunk in slowly (GS 3.86-87). The same 'crow's-beak' drinking of cool air is taught in the Śivasaṃhitā at the two twilights and day and night (ŚS 3.70, 3.74-75), and kākī is the means of filling the belly with air in vātasāra and bahiṣkṛta dhauti (GS 1.15, 1.22) and of drawing in prāṇa in yoni mudrā (GS 3.38).
signs_of_progress: destroys all diseases; one becomes free of disease like a crow (GS 3.86-87)
destroys consumption (ŚS 3.74)

warnings.text: Kākī is secret in all the tantras.

name: Bhujaṅginī mudrā ('the serpentine')
method_summary: With the mouth slightly opened and the neck stretched, air is drunk in through the gullet like a serpent (GS 3.92-93).
signs_of_progress: destroys old age and death; quickly removes diseases of the belly, especially indigestion (GS 3.92-93)

name: Drinking the breath (vāyu-pāna)
method_summary: A group of practices in the Śivasaṃhitā for removing afflictions: drinking the breath with the tongue at the root of the palate; drinking cool air through the crow's-beak mouth; drinking with the tongue pressed at the cavity of the front teeth while contemplating kuṇḍalinī; drinking with the teeth pressed together and the tongue turned up (ŚS 3.68-83); the Gorakṣaśataka similarly has the yogin press the tongue-tip at the cavity of the front teeth and contemplate the goddess of nectar (GŚ 63-64).
signs_of_progress: destroys fatigue, burning, old age and disease; claims of conquering death, becoming a poet, becoming like Bhairava with the powers (ŚS 3.71-78; GŚ 64)
notes: Where these practices merge into khecarī (the tongue turned up into the cavity) the restrictions of prc:khecari-mudra apply.

name: Ajapā-japa — the 'unrepeated' haṃsa / so'ham breath-mantra
method_summary: Attention to the breath as a mantra repeated without effort: the breath goes out with the sound 'ha' and enters with 'sa', so that the jīva repeats 'haṃsa haṃsa' — the gāyatrī called ajapā — twenty-one thousand six hundred times in a day and night (GS 5.86-88; GŚ Briggs 42-46). The Gheraṇḍa places the haṃsa in the mūlādhāra, the heart-lotus and the nostrils (GS 5.88) and relates the reach of the out-breath to the length of life (GS 5.89-92); its kevalī retention is measured against the ajapā (GS 5.93-99, restricted). Knowing this 'science of the breath' makes one a knower of yoga (GŚ Briggs 46).
signs_of_progress: freedom from all sins by merely resolving on it (GŚ Briggs 44)
notes: U04 files this under category 'mantra-sound'; it is both a breath and a sound practice. The number 21,600 is the texts' doctrinal count of daily breaths, not a practice count.

name: Svara practice: attending to the flow of breath in the nostrils (svarodaya)
method_summary: The practice of the Śiva Svarodaya: noting which channel the breath is flowing in — iḍā (left, moon), piṅgalā (right, sun) or suṣumnā (both) — as the flows alternate through the day, and timing actions accordingly: steady and auspicious acts when the moon flows, active and harsh acts when the sun flows, and only meditation and yoga when the suṣumnā flows, since worldly acts then fail. The text treats this knowledge as most secret and also teaches ways of changing the flow (not detailed here).
notes: Verse numbers of the Śiva Svarodaya not recalled; sources cite U28's topic-level teachings.

name: Discerning the elements in the breath (tattva in svara)
method_summary: Within each nostril-flow the five elements (earth, water, fire, air, space) arise in turn; the Śiva Svarodaya teaches how to recognise the element present by the length, direction, colour and taste (and shape) of the breath, and uses this knowledge, with the flows, to foretell outcomes, illness and the approach of death.
notes: Specific lengths and correspondences are not reproduced; recalled only in outline.

name: Mūlabandha (the root lock)
method_summary: Pressing the perineum with the heel and contracting the anus, the downward-moving apāna is forcibly drawn upward, again and again (HYP 3.61-63; GS 3.14-15; ŚS 4.41; DYŚ 131; GŚ 37). The Gheraṇḍa adds pressing the navel-knot toward the spine and binding the genitals with the other heel (GS 3.14-15). In breath-control it is the contraction 'below' that accompanies the throat lock (HYP 2.46).
signs_of_progress: prāṇa and apāna, nāda and bindu become one; urine and faeces diminish; the old become young (HYP 3.64-65)
the heated kuṇḍalinī awakens and enters the brahma-channel (HYP 3.66-69)
mastery of breath (GS 3.17); the yogin in padmāsana leaves the ground (ŚS 4.43)

warnings.text: To be practised in a secluded, well-hidden place, silent and free of sloth.
The one who gives the traditional instruction in the mudrās is the true guru, Īśvara himself; one practises devoted to his words.

name: Uḍḍīyānabandha (the flying-up lock)
method_summary: Drawing the belly back (paścimatāna) above and below the navel, so that the breath, bound, 'flies up' in the suṣumnā like a great bird (HYP 3.55-59; GS 3.10-11; ŚS 4.48; DYŚ 129-130; GŚ 35 places it above the penis and below the navel). In breath-control it is applied at the end of retention and the beginning of exhalation (HYP 2.45); the Gheraṇḍa applies it at the end of inhalation in sagarbha retention (GS 5.50).
signs_of_progress: the lion to the elephant of death; even the old become young; practised six months it conquers death (HYP 3.57-59; DYŚ 129-130)
the best of locks; when firm, liberation comes naturally (HYP 3.60; GS 3.11)
the navel purified, the belly-fire blazes (ŚS 4.49-50)

warnings.text: It is to be received from the guru and practised in a solitary, settled place.

name: Jālandharabandha (the throat lock)
method_summary: Contracting the throat and setting the chin firmly on the chest (HYP 3.70; GS 3.12; ŚS 4.38; DYŚ 126; GŚ 36). It binds the network of channels and the 'water of the sky', so that the nectar falling from the moon (or the thousand-petalled lotus) is not consumed by the fire at the navel; it stops the two side channels and binds the sixteen supports (HYP 3.71-73; GS 3.12; DYŚ 127-128). In breath-control it is applied at the end of inhalation (HYP 2.45).
signs_of_progress: destroys old age and death and the host of throat ailments (HYP 3.70-71)
the nectar is not burnt by the fire and the breath is not disturbed (HYP 3.72; GŚ 36)
practised six months one becomes an adept (GS 3.13)

name: The three locks together (bandha-traya)
method_summary: Mūla, uḍḍīyāna and jālandhara applied together: contracting the base, drawing back the belly and binding iḍā and piṅgalā, the breath is made to flow in the back (central) path and dissolves (HYP 3.74-76); in breath-control they are timed to inhalation, retention and exhalation (HYP 2.45-47). The texts say they arise spontaneously in a mastered siddhāsana (HYP 1.42) and that siṃhāsana brings them about (HYP 1.52).
signs_of_progress: then there is no death, old age or disease (HYP 3.75)
the means in all the haṭha teachings (HYP 3.76)

name: Mahāmudrā (the great seal)
method_summary: Pressing the perineum with the left heel, the right leg stretched out and its foot held with the hands, the chin on the chest (throat lock), the breath filled and held upward, then released slowly; practised on the left side and then equally on the right (HYP 3.10-15; GS 3.6-8; ŚS 4.16-20; DYŚ 121-122; GŚ 33). The texts say kuṇḍalinī then straightens like a snake struck with a stick and a death-like state arises as the breath leaves the two channels (HYP 3.11-12). It is the first of the trio (with mahābandha and mahāvedha) taught already in the Amṛtasiddhi.
signs_of_progress: destroys the great afflictions and death; all tastes become tasteless and even poison is digested like nectar; consumption, skin disease, constipation, gulma and indigestion vanish (HYP 3.14-17)
removes wrinkles, grey hair, old age and death, consumption, cough, fever (GS 3.8)

warnings.text: It is to be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone.
It is secret in all the tantras; to be practised as the guru teaches.
The ten mudrās are to be guarded like a jewel-box and told to no one.

notes: Homonym only of the Buddhist mahāmudrā (Kagyu); no equivalence is asserted. U04's combined entry prc:mahabandha-mahavedha overlaps the next two entries.

name: Mahābandha (the great lock)
method_summary: With the left heel at the perineum and the right foot on the left thigh, the breath is filled, the chin set firmly on the chest, the perineum contracted and the mind fixed in the middle; the breath is held as far as able and released slowly, on both sides (HYP 3.19-21; ŚS 4.21-22; DYŚ 123). In the Gheraṇḍa the left ankle blocks the anus and the right foot presses that ankle, with jālandhara (GS 3.18-20). Some teachers replace the throat lock here with the tongue pressed at the root of the front teeth (HYP 3.22).
signs_of_progress: stops the upward movement in all channels; releases death's noose; brings about the confluence of the three rivers and leads the mind to Kedāra (HYP 3.23-24)
the breath enters the middle of the suṣumnā; the body is nourished (ŚS 4.22)

warnings.text: Mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless without mahāvedha.

name: Mahāvedha (the great piercing)
method_summary: Seated in mahābandha with the breath filled and held by the throat seal, the hands placed evenly on the ground, the buttocks are gently struck on the ground so that the breath leaves the two side channels and throbs in the middle (HYP 3.26-28; ŚS 4.23; DYŚ 124, where the vulgate calls it mahābandha); in the Gheraṇḍa, a retention with uḍḍīyāna made in mahābandha (GS 3.22). Without it mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless (HYP 3.25; GS 3.21; ŚS 4.27).
signs_of_progress: a death-like state; the union of moon, sun and fire (HYP 3.28)
removes wrinkles, grey hair and trembling; gives powers such as aṇimā (HYP 3.29-30)
the brahma-knot is pierced; the gods in the centres tremble; kuṇḍalinī dissolves in Kailāsa (ŚS 4.24-26)

warnings.text: These three (mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha) are a great secret.
The best yogins keep this vedha secret.

name: Khecarī mudrā ('moving in space')
method_summary: RESTRICTED — summary only: the tongue, turned back, enters the cavity above the palate (the 'skull-cavity' or 'well of nectar') while the gaze rests between the brows (HYP 3.32; GS 3.27; ŚS 4.31; DYŚ 125; GŚ 34). The texts describe a gradual, months-long preparation of the tongue that involves cutting — not reproduced here. They also give an inner khecarī, the breath held in the void between iḍā and piṅgalā (HYP 4.43-45), and an esoteric reading of 'eating cow's flesh and drinking the liquor of the immortals' as the tongue entering the palate and drinking the moon's nectar (HYP 3.47-49). The Khecarīvidyā makes a secret mantra received from the guru essential to it.
signs_of_progress: freedom from disease, death, sloth, sleep, hunger, thirst and swoon; not stained by karma nor bound by time (HYP 3.38-40)
bindu does not fall (HYP 3.42)
the tongue tastes a succession of flavours ending in nectar (GS 3.30-32; HYP 3.50)
samādhi of the bliss of taste (GS 7.9)

warnings.text: Khecarī, like all the ten mudrās, is to be guarded like a jewel-box and told to no one.
The preparation is gradual, over months; never all at once, or the body perishes.
Learn it only from a guru who knows it from text, meaning and practice, with the mantra from the guru's mouth; keep it secret.
The practice succeeds only through the guru and the mantra together and is not to be attempted otherwise.
It is not to be given to anyone; it is to be concealed with effort.

equivalents.note: The Vivekamārtaṇḍa names the seal nabhomudrā where the Haṭhapradīpikā has khecarī; the Gheraṇḍa describes nabhomudrā as a separate, simpler practice (tongue turned up, breath held, anywhere).

name: Nabhomudrā ('the sky seal')
method_summary: Wherever one is and whatever one is doing, the tongue is kept turned upward and steady and the breath held (GS 3.9). Listed among the five seals of the Gorakṣaśataka (GŚ 32), where the Haṭhapradīpikā's list has khecarī.
signs_of_progress: destroys the yogins' diseases (GS 3.9)

name: Taḍāgī mudrā ('the tank')
method_summary: In paścimatāna, the belly is drawn back and hollowed so that it is shaped like a tank (GS 3.61).
signs_of_progress: destroys old age and death (GS 3.61)

name: Māṇḍukī mudrā ('the frog')
method_summary: With the mouth closed, the root of the tongue is moved about and the nectar slowly swallowed (GS 3.62-63).
signs_of_progress: no wrinkles or grey hair; constant youth (GS 3.63)

name: Viparītakaraṇī (the inverting technique)
method_summary: Because the sun at the navel swallows the nectar that drips from the moon at the palate, causing old age, the body is inverted — 'navel above, palate below; sun above, moon below' — the head on the ground (with the hands supporting) and the legs raised (HYP 3.77-79; GS 3.33-35; ŚS 4.45; DYŚ 133-135; GŚ 55-59). It is begun for a moment and lengthened a little day by day (HYP 3.81-82; DYŚ 135). In the Gorakṣaśataka and Vivekamārtaṇḍa it is taught as pratyāhāra, the 'withdrawal' of the nectar from the sun.
signs_of_progress: after six months wrinkles and grey hair are not seen; one who practises for a watch conquers time (HYP 3.82; DYŚ 136)
the digestive fire grows (HYP 3.80)
one does not perish even at the dissolution (GS 3.36; ŚS 4.46)

warnings.text: It increases the digestive fire, so ample food must be provided; if food is scanty the fire burns the body at once.
The same: food must be plentiful, otherwise the fire burns.
Begin with a moment on the first day and increase a little each day.
It is to be learned from the guru's instruction, not from millions of treatises.

name: Vajrolī, amarolī and sahajolī
method_summary: RESTRICTED — summary only: practices for the retention and 'drawing back' of bindu (semen, and in women rajas) through upward contraction, which the texts say let even one living as he pleases, outside the yogic rules, succeed; amarolī is ascribed to the Kāpālikas of the Khaṇḍa school and sahajolī involves smearing with ash (HYP 3.83-103; DYŚ 137-145). The Dattātreyayogaśāstra places them in the haṭha of Kapila and his followers (DYŚ 29). No procedure, material or quantity is reproduced. The Gheraṇḍa's 'vajrolī' is a different, posture-like practice (see prc:vajroli-gheranda).

warnings.text: Most secret; not to be given to anyone, only to one as dear as one's own life.
It succeeds only for the meritorious, steadfast, seers of truth and the unenvious — not for the envious.
Death comes from the fall of bindu, life from holding it; semen and mind are to be guarded with effort.
At the start of practice women, fire and travel are to be avoided.
Union with women causes loss of bindu; the yogin should avoid their company.
When women desire the yogin at the beginning stage, union destroys his bindu, shortens life and weakens him — a great obstacle.

name: Vajrolī in the Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā (the arm-supported lift)
method_summary: Supporting the ground with both hands, both legs and the head are thrown up into the air; the sages call it vajrolī, for awakening the power and for long life (GS 3.45-48).
signs_of_progress: mastery of bindu; the cause of liberation; success even for one given to enjoyment (GS 3.46-48)
notes: A different practice from the Haṭhapradīpikā's vajrolī sharing only the name and the aim of mastering bindu; not restricted.

name: Śakticālana (moving the power)
method_summary: RESTRICTED — summary only: rousing kuṇḍalinī, who sleeps coiled above the kanda covering the door of Brahman with her mouth, so that she leaves the mouth of the suṣumnā and the breath enters it (HYP 3.104-123; GS 3.49-60; ŚS 4.53-57). The texts describe it with a particular seat, pressure at the kanda, bhastrikā and contraction, or (in the Gheraṇḍa) with the navel bound in cloth and aśvinī mudrā; they call it the only means to cleanse the channels and say the yoni mudrā does not succeed without it (GS 3.57). No procedure, measure or time is reproduced.

warnings.text: Success comes to the celibate who always eats wholesome, moderate food.
It is to be practised by the guru's instruction.
It is to be kept secret and practised in a hidden room.
The ten mudrās are to be guarded like a jewel-box and told to no one.

name: Sarasvatīcālana (moving Sarasvatī)
method_summary: RESTRICTED — summary only: the 'stirring of Sarasvatī', taught with śakticālana as a means of rousing kuṇḍalinī in the (original) Gorakṣaśataka and the Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad, which say it removes abdominal disease. The procedure is not reproduced.
notes: The unit could not verify the procedure's details and deliberately gives none; the Mallinson 'original' Gorakṣaśataka is not available locally.

name: Yoni mudrā (the womb seal)
method_summary: In the Gheraṇḍa: seated in siddhāsana, the ears, eyes, nostrils and mouth are closed with the fingers, prāṇa is drawn in by kākī and joined with apāna, the six centres are contemplated in order with the mantra 'huṃ haṃsa', the sleeping serpent-goddess is roused and led with the jīva to the supreme lotus, and one contemplates union with Śiva — 'I am Brahman' (GS 3.37-42); it is the means to laya-samādhi (GS 7.12-13). In the Śivasaṃhitā it is the contraction of the yoni between anus and genitals with meditation on the flame rising from the brahma-yoni (ŚS 4.1-11), perfected by mūlabandha (ŚS 4.42). The Haṭhapradīpikā mentions it as holding bindu (HYP 3.43).
signs_of_progress: one established in it even once is in samādhi (GS 3.42)
makes defective mantras effective (ŚS 4.6)

warnings.text: Yoni mudrā does not succeed without first practising śakticālana.
It is most secret; it is not to be given to anyone, not even with one's life in one's throat.

equivalents.note: The Gheraṇḍa's yoni mudrā includes the closing of the six openings that is elsewhere the whole of ṣaṇmukhī; the Śivasaṃhitā's yoni mudrā is a perineal contraction.

notes: The texts' claims that it removes even the great sins are arthavāda in their own manner.

name: Aśvinī mudrā ('the mare')
method_summary: Contracting and expanding the anal opening again and again (GS 3.82-83); it is used in dry basti and in śakticālanī (GS 1.48, 3.55).
signs_of_progress: awakens the power; destroys diseases of the anus; gives strength and nourishment; prevents untimely death (GS 3.82-83)

name: Pāśinī mudrā ('the noose')
method_summary: Both legs are thrown behind the neck and held firmly like a noose (GS 3.84-85).
signs_of_progress: awakens the power; gives strength and nourishment (GS 3.84-85)

name: Śāmbhavī mudrā (Śambhu's seal)
method_summary: The inner target held while the gaze is outward and unblinking — looking yet not seeing, with mind and breath dissolved in the inner target (HYP 4.36-37); in the Gheraṇḍa, looking at the point between the eyes and beholding the self (GS 3.64). It is the means to dhyāna-samādhi (GS 7.5-8) and to subtle meditation (GS 6.21); trāṭaka leads to it (GS 1.54); śāmbhavī is held while listening to the inner sound (HYP 4.67).
signs_of_progress: the reality, Śambhu's state beyond void and non-void, shines forth (HYP 4.37)
one who knows it is Ādinātha, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā — is Brahman (GS 3.66-67)

warnings.text: It is obtained by the guru's grace.
The Vedas, śāstras and purāṇas are like common courtesans; śāmbhavī is guarded like a woman of good family.

equivalents.note: Śāṇḍilya Up. 1.31 defines vaiṣṇavī mudrā in the very terms by which HYP 4.36 defines śāmbhavī (inner target, outward unblinking gaze).

name: Ṣaṇmukhī mudrā (closing the six openings)
method_summary: Closing the ears, eyes, nostrils and mouth with the fingers — in the Śivasaṃhitā the thumbs close the ears, the index fingers the eyes, the middle fingers the nostrils and the ring fingers the mouth — while the breath is restrained, so that the self is seen as light and then the inner sound arises (ŚS 5.22-26; HYP 4.68, where the practice is not named; GS 3.37 within yoni mudrā; Yogacūḍāmaṇi 114-115).
signs_of_progress: the self is seen as light; the sinner is freed; the body is forgotten (ŚS 5.22-24)
a clear, pure sound is heard in the purified suṣumnā (HYP 4.68)
sounds like bells (Yogacūḍāmaṇi 114-115)

warnings.text: It is to be practised secretly (guptācāreṇa).

notes: The name ṣaṇmukhī for HYP 4.68 comes from Brahmānanda's commentary (recalled). U04 filed the same practice as prc:shanmukhi-mudra (non-IAST slug); the two ids should be merged into this one.

name: Ritual hand-gestures (hasta-mudrā) in worship
method_summary: Gestures of the hands made at fixed points of worship, mantra-repetition and meditation, which 'give joy' (mudaṃ rāti) to the deities and make them present; the fingers are held to be the five elements (little finger earth … thumb space) whose joinings produce the gestures. The Śāradātilaka gives the invocation series (āvāhanī and the rest), avaguṇṭhana, dhenu and mahāmudrā (ŚT 23.106-114) and its commentary many more (aṅkuśa, kumbha, śaṅkha, garuḍa, jñāna, weapon-gestures of the deities).

warnings.text: The mudrās are not to be shown in a crowd or to the uninitiated; for seekers of liberation they may be made mentally.

name: The invocation gestures (āvāhanī and the rest)
method_summary: The series by which a deity is invited and settled in worship: āvāhanī (the añjali filled with flowers), sthāpanī (the same turned downward), sannidhāpanī (the fists joined, thumbs raised), sannirodhanī (the same with thumbs inside), sammukhīkaraṇī (the fists turned up), with sakalīkaraṇa (placing the six limbs on the deity), avaguṇṭhana (the right fist with the index finger extended, turned around), dhenu (amṛtīkaraṇa) and mahāmudrā (paramīkaraṇa) (ŚT 23.106-114).

name: Dhenu mudrā (the cow gesture)
method_summary: The little and ring fingers, and the index and middle fingers, of the two hands interlaced and joined facing each other; with it the officiant turns the offering-water into nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa) (ŚT 23.112-113, with the commentary's fuller description).

name: Mahāmudrā as a hand-gesture (paramīkaraṇa)
method_summary: The thumbs interlocked and the fingers extended, shown to 'make supreme' (paramīkaraṇa) in the worship of the deity (ŚT 23.113-114); distinct from the haṭha mahāmudrā.

name: Aṅkuśa mudrā (the goad gesture)
method_summary: The middle finger of the left fist, held in the right fist, extended and the index bent like a goad; used to draw the sacred waters (tīrtha) from the sun's disc into the bathing water (Śāradātilaka ch. 4, in Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary).

name: Śaṅkha mudrā (the conch gesture)
method_summary: The left thumb grasped in the right fist, the right thumb extended and the remaining left fingers joined and stretched to touch it — the conch, shown over the arghya vessel (Śāradātilaka ch. 4 commentary; 'śaṅkhamudrāṃ pradarśya' in the arghya rite).

name: Garuḍa mudrā
method_summary: The hands facing each other, the little fingers and the index fingers joined, the thumbs joined, the middle and ring fingers bent like wings — said to destroy all poison; shown in Vaiṣṇava worship (Śāradātilaka ch. 4 commentary).

name: Jñāna mudrā / cin-mudrā (the gesture of knowledge)
method_summary: The tips of thumb and index finger joined and the other fingers extended, turned to the side — the gesture of knowledge held by teaching deities such as Sarasvatī and Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the commentary distinguishes a related 'exposition gesture' (vyākhyāna-mudrā) (Śāradātilaka, commentary on ch. 6 and ch. 7).

name: Yoni mudrā as a hand-gesture in Śākta worship
method_summary: A gesture of the hands forming the yoni, shown to the goddess after meditation in Śākta worship (named repeatedly in the Śāradātilaka's rites, e.g. with the śaṅkha, cakra and mahāmudrā); distinct from the haṭha yoni mudrā.
notes: The form of the gesture is not described here; its details were not verified.

name: Añjali mudrā (the joined palms)
method_summary: The palms joined, as the gesture of homage; placed at the forehead it is the gesture of salutation (vandana-mudrā), and in Vaiṣṇava worship the añjali is called the Vāsudeva gesture (Śāradātilaka commentary).

name: Abhaya and varada mudrā (the gestures of fearlessness and boon-giving)
method_summary: The raised open palm that grants fearlessness (abhaya) and the lowered open palm that grants boons (varada), held by deities in the meditation-verses (dhyāna) of the Śāradātilaka and shown by the worshipper after meditation ('varābhaya…mudrāḥ pradarśayet'); the same pair is standard in Buddhist and Jain images.
notes: Buddhist and Jain iconographic use is noted; those units own their fuller treatment.

name: Dhauti (washing) — the class of cleansing acts
method_summary: The first of the six acts. In the Haṭhapradīpikā dhauti is the swallowing and withdrawing of a moistened cloth (HYP 2.24-25). In the Gheraṇḍa dhauti is fourfold — inner (antar-dhauti: vātasāra, vārisāra, vahnisāra, bahiṣkṛta), of the teeth (danta-dhauti: tooth-roots, tongue, ears, the forehead hollow), of the heart/chest (hṛd-dhauti: with a stick, by vomiting, with a cloth) and of the root (mūlaśodhana) — and it cleans the body (GS 1.13-44). The Gheraṇḍa also counts dhauti as the nirmanu way of purifying the channels (GS 5.36).

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.
Some teachers hold that all impurities are dried up by breath-control alone and do not approve of the other acts.
The six acts, which purify the body, are to be kept secret.
The Śivasaṃhitā counts washing by dhauti (with sitting in gomukha, stirring the belly and the like) among the obstacles that take the form of knowledge.

name: Vastra-dhauti (washing with a cloth; vāso-dhauti)
method_summary: A moistened strip of fine cloth is slowly swallowed as the guru teaches and then drawn out again (HYP 2.24; GS 1.40). The measurements the texts give are not reproduced.
signs_of_progress: cough, asthma, spleen disorders, skin disease and the twenty diseases of phlegm vanish (HYP 2.25)
gulma, fever, spleen disorders, skin disease, phlegm and bile destroyed; health, strength and nourishment increase (GS 1.41)

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.
Some teachers hold that all impurities are dried up by breath-control alone and do not approve of the other acts.
The six acts, which purify the body, are to be kept secret.
Dhauti is done 'by the way the guru teaches'.

name: Vātasāra (inner washing with air)
method_summary: With the mouth shaped like a crow's beak (kākī) air is slowly drunk, moved in the belly and released slowly by the lower passage (GS 1.15-16).
signs_of_progress: cleans the body, destroys all diseases, increases the bodily fire (GS 1.16)

warnings.text: Vātasāra is most secret.

name: Vārisāra (inner washing with water)
method_summary: Water is drunk slowly until the body is filled to the throat, moved through the belly and expelled downward (GS 1.17-19).
signs_of_progress: cleans the body; one who practises it with effort gains a divine body (GS 1.18-19)

warnings.text: Vārisāra is most secret.

notes: Later (recent) teaching calls a comparable practice śaṅkhaprakṣālana; that name is not in the Gheraṇḍa.

name: Vahnisāra / agnisāra (inner washing by fire)
method_summary: The navel-knot is pressed back toward the spine repeatedly (the count is not reproduced) (GS 1.20-21).
signs_of_progress: removes abdominal disorders and increases the digestive fire; by it alone the body becomes divine (GS 1.20-21)

warnings.text: This dhauti is most secret and never to be revealed.

name: Bahiṣkṛta-dhauti (the outward washing)
method_summary: RESTRICTED — summary only: described as filling the belly with air by kākī mudrā and holding it, then, standing in navel-deep water, drawing out and washing the 'śakti-nāḍī' (the lower bowel) and returning it (GS 1.22-25). Procedure and durations are not reproduced.

warnings.text: This washing is secret and hard to attain even for the gods.
The great bahiṣkṛta-dhauti does not arise until one can hold (the air) for a long period.

name: Dantamūla-dhauti (cleansing the roots of the teeth)
method_summary: The roots of the teeth are rubbed with catechu juice or pure earth until the impurity is removed, daily at dawn (GS 1.27-28).
signs_of_progress: protects the teeth (GS 1.28)

name: Jihvā-śodhana (cleansing — and lengthening — the tongue)
method_summary: The root of the tongue is cleaned with three fingers inserted into the throat to remove phlegm (GS 1.30). RESTRICTED in part: the text goes on to describe rubbing the tongue with butter, 'milking' it and drawing it out with an iron instrument daily at sunrise so that it lengthens (GS 1.31-32) — a preparation for khecarī; that procedure is not reproduced.
signs_of_progress: the text says a long tongue destroys old age, death and disease (GS 1.29)

warnings.text: Khecarī and its preparation are to be learnt only from a qualified guru and done gradually.

name: Karṇa-dhauti (cleansing the ears)
method_summary: The openings of the ears are cleaned with the tips of the index and ring fingers (GS 1.33).
signs_of_progress: by daily practice the inner sound becomes manifest (GS 1.33)

name: Kapālarandhra-dhauti (rubbing the forehead hollow)
method_summary: The hollow at the forehead (bhālarandhra) is rubbed with the right thumb, on waking, after meals and at the end of the day (GS 1.34-35).
signs_of_progress: removes phlegm; the channels become clean and divine sight arises (GS 1.34-35)

name: Daṇḍa-dhauti (washing with a stick)
method_summary: A stalk of plantain, turmeric or cane is moved within the chest (gullet) and slowly withdrawn, expelling phlegm, bile and mucus upward (GS 1.37-38).
signs_of_progress: destroys heart disease (GS 1.38)

name: Vamana-dhauti (washing by vomiting)
method_summary: After a meal water is drunk to the throat, the gaze turned upward for a moment, and the water vomited (GS 1.39).
signs_of_progress: removes phlegm and bile (GS 1.39)
notes: Recent teaching calls a comparable practice kuñjala; that name is not in the Gheraṇḍa.

equivalents.note: Both empty the stomach upward; gajakaraṇī does it by raising apāna to the throat, vamana-dhauti after drinking water.

name: Mūlaśodhana (cleansing the root)
method_summary: The anus is washed with water again and again, using a stalk of turmeric or the middle finger (GS 1.42-44).
signs_of_progress: removes the 'harshness' of apāna, hardness of the bowels and indigestion; gives beauty and nourishment; kindles the fire (GS 1.42-44)

equivalents.note: Both cleanse the anus with the finger; the Haṭharatnāvalī names its act cakrī.

name: Basti / jala-basti (the water enema)
method_summary: Squatting in utkaṭāsana in water up to the navel with a tube in the anus, one contracts the base (ādhāra) and washes (HYP 2.26-28); the Gheraṇḍa's water-basti is done likewise in navel-deep water with contraction and expansion of the anus (GS 1.45-47).
signs_of_progress: gulma, spleen disorders, dropsy and diseases of vāta, pitta and kapha are destroyed; clarity of tissues, senses and mind; lustre; kindled fire (HYP 2.27-28)
removes urinary disorders, gudāvarta and harsh wind (GS 1.47)

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.
Some teachers hold that all impurities are dried up by breath-control alone and do not approve of the other acts.
The six acts, which purify the body, are to be kept secret.

name: Śuṣka-basti (the dry basti)
method_summary: Done on the ground in paścimatāna, moving (the belly) slowly and contracting and expanding the anus with aśvinī mudrā (GS 1.48-49).
signs_of_progress: no bowel disorders; increased digestive fire; destroys āmavāta (GS 1.49)

name: Neti (the nasal thread)
method_summary: A smooth, fine thread is passed into a nostril and drawn out through the mouth (HYP 2.29; GS 1.50). The measurement the texts give is not reproduced.
signs_of_progress: cleanses the skull, gives divine sight, destroys diseases above the collar-bones (HYP 2.30)
gives khecarī-siddhi, removes phlegm disorders, gives divine sight (GS 1.51)

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.
Some teachers hold that all impurities are dried up by breath-control alone and do not approve of the other acts.
The six acts, which purify the body, are to be kept secret.

notes: 'Sūtra-neti' and 'jala-neti' (with water) are later names; the Gheraṇḍa's vyutkrama kapālabhāti draws water through the nose.

name: Trāṭaka (the fixed gaze)
method_summary: With steady eyes and concentrated mind, one gazes without blinking at a small target until tears fall (HYP 2.31; GS 1.53). Listed by the texts among the six acts, it is also a practice of concentration: in the Gheraṇḍa it leads to śāmbhavī (GS 1.54).
signs_of_progress: frees from eye diseases and bars sloth (HYP 2.32)
śāmbhavī arises; no eye disease; divine sight (GS 1.54)

warnings.text: To be guarded as carefully as a golden casket.
One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.

notes: The texts name only a 'small target' (sūkṣma-lakṣya); gazing at a candle flame is later usage (recent teachers).

name: Nauli / laulikī (churning the belly)
method_summary: With the shoulders bent forward the belly is turned to the right and left with great speed, like a whirlpool (HYP 2.33; GS 1.52 laulikī).
signs_of_progress: kindles weak digestive fire, aids digestion, brings joy, dries up all disorders — the crown of the haṭha practices (HYP 2.34)
destroys all diseases and increases the bodily fire (GS 1.52)

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.
Some teachers hold that all impurities are dried up by breath-control alone and do not approve of the other acts.
The six acts, which purify the body, are to be kept secret.

name: Kapālabhāti / bhālabhāti (the skull-shining)
method_summary: In the Haṭhapradīpikā, rapid exhalation and inhalation like a blacksmith's bellows (HYP 2.35). In the Gheraṇḍa bhālabhāti is threefold: vāmakrama (breathing through alternate nostrils, not forcefully), vyutkrama (water drawn in through the nose and expelled through the mouth) and śītkrama (water sucked in through the mouth and expelled through the nose) (GS 1.55-60).
signs_of_progress: dries up the disorders of phlegm (HYP 2.35; GS 1.55)

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.
Some teachers hold that all impurities are dried up by breath-control alone and do not approve of the other acts.
The six acts, which purify the body, are to be kept secret.

name: Vāmakrama bhālabhāti (alternate-nostril form)
method_summary: Breathing in through iḍā and out through piṅgalā, then in through piṅgalā and out through iḍā, without force (GS 1.56-57).
signs_of_progress: removes phlegm disorders (GS 1.57)

warnings.text: One should not do it forcefully.

name: Vyutkrama bhālabhāti (water through the nose)
method_summary: Water is drawn in through the nostrils and expelled through the mouth, again and again (GS 1.58).
signs_of_progress: removes disorders of phlegm (GS 1.58)

name: Śītkrama bhālabhāti (water through the mouth)
method_summary: Water is sucked in through the mouth with a hissing sound and expelled through the nose (GS 1.59-60).
signs_of_progress: one becomes like the god of love; no old age or fever; the body free; phlegm disorders removed (GS 1.59-60)

name: Gajakaraṇī ('the elephant's act')
method_summary: Raising the apāna breath to the throat, one vomits what is in the stomach; by gradual practice the wheel of channels comes under control (HYP 2.38). The Haṭharatnāvalī counts it among its eight acts.

warnings.text: One with excess fat or phlegm should first practise the six acts; others should not do them, their doṣas being in balance.

name: Cakrī (the 'wheel' act)
method_summary: One of the eight cleansing acts of the Haṭharatnāvalī, added to the Haṭhapradīpikā's six (with gajakaraṇī); it is a cleansing of the anus — the unit recalls it as done by rotating the finger there, like the Gheraṇḍa's mūlaśodhana.
notes: Method recalled with low confidence; check the Haṭharatnāvalī.

name: Mātaṅginī mudrā ('the elephant')
method_summary: Standing in water up to the neck, water is drawn in through the nostrils and expelled through the mouth, then drawn in through the mouth and expelled through the nostrils, again and again (GS 3.88-91). Counted by the Gheraṇḍa among its twenty-five mudrās.
signs_of_progress: destroys old age and death; one becomes strong like an elephant and enjoys great happiness (GS 3.89-91)

warnings.text: To be practised in a secluded, uninhabited place with a one-pointed mind.
